Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. Write $K_i:=K_{d_i h_i}$ and $K_i^{-1}:=K_{-d_i h_i}$. Let $V$ be the $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector space with basis the symbols $\{E_i,F_i\}_{i\in I}\cup\{K_h\}_{h\in P^{\vee}}$, and let $T:=T(V)$ be its free unital associative $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]], [[thm-universal-property-of-the-tensor-algebra]]). Let $I_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ be the two-sided ideal of $T$ generated by ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]) the following relations:

$$K_0-1,\qquad K_hK_{h'}-K_{h+h'}\qquad(h,h'\in P^{\vee});$$

$$K_hE_i-q^{\langle\alpha_i,h\rangle}E_iK_h,\qquad K_hF_i-q^{-\langle\alpha_i,h\rangle}F_iK_h\qquad(h\in P^{\vee},\ i\in I);$$

$$E_iF_j-F_jE_i-\delta_{ij}\frac{K_i-K_i^{-1}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}\qquad(i,j\in I);$$

$$\mathrm{Serre}^+_{ij}:=\sum_{r=0}^{1-a_{ij}}(-1)^r\binom{1-a_{ij}}{r}_iE_i^{1-a_{ij}-r}E_jE_i^r,\qquad \mathrm{Serre}^-_{ij}:=\sum_{r=0}^{1-a_{ij}}(-1)^r\binom{1-a_{ij}}{r}_iF_i^{1-a_{ij}-r}F_jF_i^r\qquad(i\ne j),$$

where the Gaussian binomials are those of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. The **Drinfeld-Jimbo quantized enveloping algebra** is

$$U_q(\mathfrak g):=T/I_{\mathrm{DJ}}$$

([[def-quotient-ring]]), with $E_i,F_i,K_h$ denoting the images of the generators. In this quotient, $K_i^{-1}$ is the two-sided inverse of $K_i$.

It is graded by the root lattice $Q=\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\alpha_i$ ([[def-kac-moody-root-lattice-height-and-positive-cone]]), with $\deg E_i=\alpha_i$, $\deg F_i=-\alpha_i$ and $\deg K_h=0$; thus $U_q(\mathfrak g)=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q}U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]$.

For every unital associative $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra $B$, any assignment of elements $E_i',F_i',K_h'\in B$ satisfying these relations extends uniquely to a $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra homomorphism $U_q(\mathfrak g)\to B$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-universal-property]]).

Let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]] with its root-lattice grading $U_q(\mathfrak g)=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q}U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]$. Define

$$U_q^+:=\langle E_i\ :\ i\in I\rangle,\qquad U_q^-:=\langle F_i\ :\ i\in I\rangle,\qquad U_q^0:=\langle K_h\ :\ h\in P^{\vee}\rangle,$$

the $\mathbb Q(q)$-subalgebras generated by the indicated images, and let $Q_+=\bigoplus_i\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$. Then

$$U_q^\pm=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q_+}U_q^\pm[\pm\beta],\qquad U_q^+[\beta]:=U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]\cap U_q^+,\quad U_q^-[ -\beta]:=U_q(\mathfrak g)[-\beta]\cap U_q^-.$$

The degree-zero component $U_q(\mathfrak g)[0]$ contains $U_q^0$, and for every $x\in U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]$ and $h\in P^{\vee}$,

$$K_hxK_h^{-1}=q^{\beta(h)}x.$$

Thus each $K_h\in U_q^0$ acts by conjugation on the degree-$\beta$ component as the scalar $q^{\beta(h)}$. The elements $K_h$ span $U_q^0$ and satisfy $K_hK_{h'}=K_{h+h'}$ with $K_0=1$; hence $U_q^0$ is a quotient of the group algebra $\mathbb Q(q)[P^{\vee}]$. The subalgebras $U_q^\pm$ are spanned by finite monomials in the $E_i$ and $F_i$, respectively. Define the nonnegative and nonpositive product spans by

$$U_q^{\ge0}:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q(q)}(U_q^0U_q^+),\qquad U_q^{\le0}:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q(q)}(U_q^-U_q^0).$$

This definition asserts no linear independence of these spanning families and no injectivity of the natural maps; those claims belong to [[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]].

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. For $m\in\mathbb N$, define the **$q_i$-integer**

$$[m]_i:=\frac{q_i^m-q_i^{-m}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}},\qquad [0]_i:=0,$$

and the **$q_i$-factorial**

$$[m]_i!:=\prod_{k=1}^m[k]_i,\qquad [0]_i!:=1.$$

For $0\le r\le m$, define the **Gaussian binomial** $\binom{m}{r}_i:=[m]_i!/([r]_i![m-r]_i!)$, and set it to $0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$. In the published one-parameter convention, write $\binom{m}{r}_t:=\binom{m}{r,m-r}_t$ for the two-part $q$-multinomial coefficient of [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]].

For an element $x$ of a unital $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and $m\ge0$, define its **divided power at $q_i$** by $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$, so $x^{(0)}=1$ and $x^{(1)}=x$.

The symmetric convention and the published asymmetric convention are related, for $m\ge0$ and $0\le r\le m$, by

$$[m]_i=q_i^{-(m-1)}[m]_{q_i^2},\qquad \binom{m}{r}_i=q_i^{-r(m-r)}\binom{m}{r}_{q_i^2}.$$

In particular $[m]_i$ is invariant under $q_i\mapsto q_i^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the symmetrizer only through $q_i=q^{d_i}$.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum
group with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]) with $q_i=q^{d_i}$ and
$K_i=K_{d_ih_i}$, and set

$$A:=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\ \subseteq\ \mathbb Q(q),$$

the image of the Laurent polynomial ring $\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t]_{S}$ of
[[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]] under the unital ring homomorphism sending
$t$ to the indeterminate $q$; this homomorphism is injective and $A$ is a
subring of $\mathbb Q(q)$ (Verification, step 1.1). We work over this
commutative domain $A$ inside the field $\mathbb Q(q)$.

For $i\in I$, $c\in\mathbb Z$ and $t\ge0$ define the **toral quantum binomial**

$$T_{i,c,t}:=\begin{bmatrix}K_i;c\\ t\end{bmatrix}:=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\frac{K_iq_i^{\,c-s+1}-K_i^{-1}q_i^{\,-c+s-1}}{q_i^{\,s}-q_i^{\,-s}}\in U_q(\mathfrak g),$$

the empty product being $T_{i,c,0}:=1$. Each factor is defined in
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ because $q_i^{\,s}-q_i^{\,-s}\ne0$ for $s\ge1$
([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]), so
$T_{i,c,t}$ is a polynomial in $K_i^{\pm1}$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$;
in particular all $T_{i,c,t}$ commute with the $K_h$ and with one another
(Verification, step 2.1).

The **Lusztig divided-power integral form** is the $A$-subalgebra

$$U_A:=\bigl\langle E_i^{(r)},\ F_i^{(r)},\ K_h^{\pm1},\ T_{i,c,t}\ \colon\ i\in I,\ r,t\ge0,\ c\in\mathbb Z,\ h\in P^{\vee}\bigr\rangle\ \subseteq\ U_q(\mathfrak g),$$

where $x^{(r)}=x^r/[r]_i!$ are the divided powers of
[[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $U_A^\pm$
for the $A$-subalgebras generated by the $E_i^{(r)}$ and by the $F_i^{(r)}$,
and $U_A^0$ for the one generated by the $K_h^{\pm1}$ and the $T_{i,c,t}$.

Then:

(i) $U_A$ contains $E_i=E_i^{(1)}$, $F_i=F_i^{(1)}$ and all $K_h$;

(ii) $U_A$ is a root-graded $A$-subalgebra of the root-graded
$\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]):
with $U_A[\beta]:=U_A\cap U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]$ one has
$U_A=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q}U_A[\beta]$, each $U_A[\beta]$ is an $A$-submodule,
and $U_A^\pm,U_A^0$ are graded in the same way;

(iii) $U_A\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)\cong U_q(\mathfrak g)$ canonically, i.e. the
$\mathbb Q(q)$-span of $U_A$ is all of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$.

The shifted binomials $T_{i,c,t}$ with $c\ne0$ are included because the
divided-power reordering identity of
[[lem-divided-power-and-toral-quantum-binomial-reordering-identities]] has
coefficients $T_{i,2t-a-b,t}$ with a nonconstant index; the specializations at
$q=1$ of these elements are computed in
[[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]],
and the integral triangular decomposition and the specialization are treated
only after this definition.

No freeness of $U_A$ or of its parts over $A$, no independence of the listed
generators, and no triangularity of the products of the three parts is asserted
here. In particular $A$ is not a principal ideal domain (Verification, step
7.1), so no torsion-free-to-free inference over $A$ is permitted anywhere on
this page.

Fix $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$ and the crystal limiting ring $A_0\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$ of [[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]], and put $A_\infty:=\psi(A_0)$, the image of $A_0$ under the semilinear involution $\psi(q)=q^{-1}$, i.e. the ring of rational functions regular at $q=\infty$; $A_0$ and $A_\infty$ are the rational local rings at $0$ and at infinity, and the integral affine chart coordinate rings are $\mathbb Z[q]$ and $\mathbb Z[q^{-1}]$.

Let $M$ be one of $U_q^-$ or $V(\lambda)=L(\lambda)$ for $\lambda\in P^+$. Equip $M$ with the bar involution $\psi$ of [[lem-the-lusztig-integral-form-is-stable-under-bar-and-contravariant-duality]]: on $U_q^-$ the semilinear algebra involution with $\psi(q)=q^{-1}$, $\psi(E_i)=E_i$, $\psi(F_i)=F_i$, $\psi(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$; on $V(\lambda)$ the induced semilinear involution determined by $Pv_\lambda\mapsto\psi(P)v_\lambda$, well defined because the highest weight vector is fixed. Let $M_A\subseteq M$ be the divided-power integral form: $M_A=U_A^-$ for $M=U_q^-$, and $M_A=V_A(\lambda):=U_A^-v_\lambda$ for $M=V(\lambda)$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]); both are $\psi$-stable. Let $L$ be the Kashiwara crystal lattice of $M$ over $A_0$: $L=\mathcal L(\infty)$ for $U_q^-$ and $L=\mathcal L(\lambda)$ for $V(\lambda)$ ([[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]], [[thm-grand-loop-existence-of-highest-weight-crystal-bases]]).

Define the **bar lattice** $L^-:=\psi(L)$, an $A_\infty$-submodule of $M$, and the **balanced part** $E:=M_A\cap L\cap L^-$.

The definition keeps three structures on the same $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector space strictly separate: the $A$-module $M_A$, which is not assumed free and not claimed to be contained in $L$; the free $A_0$-module $L$; and the free $A_\infty$-module $L^-$. No equality $L^-=L$, no inclusion $M_A\subseteq L$, no freeness of $M_A$ and no identification $E=M_A$ are asserted; freeness is a conclusion of the balanced-triple construction on this page, whereas $E$ is a $\mathbb Z$-module of global lifts and is not equal to the Laurent lattice $M_A$. The bar lattice is not the form-dual (upper) lattice, which is defined later on this page. The intersections $M_A\cap L$ and $M_A\cap L^-$ are respectively $\mathbb Z[q]$- and $\mathbb Z[q^{-1}]$-modules, generally not $A$-modules. The balanced part $E$ is a $\mathbb Z$-module; its Laurent extension $A\otimes_{\mathbb Z}E$ is the full integral module once globalization is proved.

More generally a **based integrable module** $(M,B)$ here means exactly: $B$ is a homogeneous field basis; $M_A=\bigoplus_bAb$ is $U_A$-stable; the semilinear involution fixing $B$ is compatible with the algebra action; and $L_0=\bigoplus_bA_0b$ with residue $B$ is a crystal local basis at $0$. These are the four conditions of Lusztig 27.1.2(a)–(d) after the transport $v=q^{-1}$, together with the integrable extension used by Bao–Wang. Such data do not automatically imply an integral $\Theta$-action on an arbitrary based pair. A **based subobject** is a $U$-submodule spanned by a subset of $B$; a **based quotient** is its quotient with the complementary basis images. Based morphisms send $B$ to the target basis or to $0$, and have kernels spanned by the killed basis subset. These exact integral and bar-compatible maps, not arbitrary field summands, are used in tensor inheritance.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum with $a_{ii}=2$ for
all $i$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). The **linear
contravariant anti-involution** $\sigma$ of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ is defined on
generators by

$$\sigma(q)=q,\qquad\sigma(K_h)=K_h,\qquad\sigma(E_i)=q_iF_iK_i^{-1},\qquad\sigma(F_i)=q_i^{-1}K_iE_i,$$

extended as an anti-algebra map, $\sigma(xy)=\sigma(y)\sigma(x)$. It is
$\mathbb Q(q)$-linear, preserves the torus (it does not invert it), and is an
involution (Verification, step 1.1). It is distinct from the semilinear
contravariant anti-involution $\tau$ with $\tau(q)=q^{-1}$,
$\tau(E_i)=F_i$, $\tau(F_i)=E_i$, $\tau(K_h)=K_{-h}$ of
[[lem-quantum-serre-relations-are-stable-under-the-chevalley-involutions]].

Let $\lambda\in P$ be dominant integral ([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]),
so $\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$ for all $i$, and let $(M,v_\lambda)$ be a
**normalized highest weight module**: $M$ is a $P$-graded type-one quantum
weight module ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) with
$v_\lambda\in M_\lambda$, $E_iv_\lambda=0$ for all $i$, and $M=U_q(\mathfrak g)v_\lambda$.
(The normalized simple highest weight module $L(\lambda)$ is the companion
construction later on this page; the present definition applies to any
normalized highest weight module, in particular to the Verma module and to its
simple quotient.)

A **contravariant form** on $(M,v_\lambda)$ is a bilinear form
$B\colon M\times M\to\mathbb Q(q)$ such that

(i) $B$ is symmetric: $B(u,v)=B(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in M$;

(ii) $B$ is **homogeneous** for the label grading: $B(M_\mu,M_\tau)=0$
whenever the two labels have different toral characters, that is, whenever
$\langle\mu,h\rangle\ne\langle\tau,h\rangle$ for some $h\in P^{\vee}$;

(iii) $B(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$ (the normalization);

(iv) $B$ is $\sigma$-invariant: $B(xu,v)=B(u,\sigma(x)v)$ for all
$x\in U_q(\mathfrak g)$ and all $u,v\in M$.

Because $\sigma$ is $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear and fixes the torus, condition (iv)
is equivalent to the adjunction displays

$$B(K_hu,v)=B(u,K_hv),\qquad B(E_iu,v)=B(u,q_iF_iK_i^{-1}v),\qquad B(F_iu,v)=B(u,q_i^{-1}K_iE_iv),$$

for all $u,v\in M$, $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $i\in I$ (Verification, step 2.1).

For $\lambda$ dominant and $L(\lambda)$ the normalized simple highest weight
module, such a form exists, is unique, and is nondegenerate on $L(\lambda)$;
moreover distinct label-weight spaces with distinct characters are orthogonal
by (ii). Uniqueness is proved here (Verification, step 4.1), as is the
orthogonality; consequently, when the pairing separates $P$, the distinct
label-weight spaces of $L(\lambda)$ are orthogonal and the restriction of $B$
to each finite-dimensional label-weight space is nondegenerate (Verification,
step 5.1). The
existence, the identification of the radical on the Verma module and the
descent to $L(\lambda)$ are proved in the local Cartan-projection lemma
`lem-cartan-projection-constructs-the-quantum-verma-contravariant-form`, which
is the declared justification of this definition. That lemma is proved on this
page, and its statement is the supplier of the existence and nondegeneracy
clauses above; establishing those clauses is its content rather than a claim of
this definition.

Let $\lambda\in P^+$ and let $L(\lambda)$ be the simple integrable highest weight module with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$ ([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]); in this page we write $V(\lambda):=L(\lambda)$, following the notation of the crystal sources. Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half with its Kashiwara operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]), and let $A_0$ be the crystal limiting ring ([[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]]).

Define $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ to be the $A_0$-submodule of $V(\lambda)$ generated by all vectors $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda$ ($r\ge0$, $i_1,\dots,i_r\in I$), where for $r=0$ the vector is $v_\lambda$; and $\mathcal L(\infty)$ to be the $A_0$-submodule of $U_q^-$ generated by all $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}\mathbf 1$ ($r\ge0$), where $\mathbf 1$ is the unit of $U_q^-$. Here $\tilde f_i$ on $V(\lambda)$ are the module Kashiwara operators and $\tilde f_i$ on $U_q^-$ are the negative-half operators. Define
$$\mathcal B(\lambda):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda+q\mathcal L(\lambda):r\ge0\}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)/q\mathcal L(\lambda),$$
$$\mathcal B(\infty):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}\mathbf 1+q\mathcal L(\infty):r\ge0\}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)/q\mathcal L(\infty).$$

Then, with $\pi_\lambda:U_q^-\to V(\lambda)$, $\pi_\lambda(P)=Pv_\lambda$:

(a) $\mathcal L(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu$ with $\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu=\mathcal L(\lambda)\cap V(\lambda)_\mu$, and $\mathcal L(\infty)=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}$ with $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}=\mathcal L(\infty)\cap U_q^-[-\nu]$; correspondingly $\mathcal B(\lambda)=\bigsqcup_\mu\mathcal B(\lambda)_\mu$ and $\mathcal B(\infty)=\bigsqcup_\nu\mathcal B(\infty)_{-\nu}$.

(b) $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)$ and $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\infty)\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)$.

(c) (Recursive spanning.) For $\alpha\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$,
$$\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\sum_{i\in I}\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i},\qquad \mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\tilde f_i\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i}\Bigr)\setminus\{0\},$$
and the same formulas with $\mathcal L(\infty),\mathcal B(\infty)$. Each $\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$ and each $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha}$ is generated over $A_0$ by finitely many monomials of total length at most $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$, hence is a finitely generated $A_0$-module.

No basis property, scalar-extension spanning or crystal-lattice property of $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ or $\mathcal L(\infty)$ is asserted here; these are conclusions of the grand loop. The script letters avoid the collision with the simple module $L(\lambda)$. No choice principle is used. Each fixed component is torsionfree inside a field vector space and generated by finitely many words of its fixed height, so it is free over the DVR $A_0$; its full field-span is proved later. The field map $\pi_\lambda$ is surjective, but exact equality on Kashiwara monomial generators is not asserted.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group
with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), with root lattice $Q$,
simple roots $\alpha_i\in P$ and integer pairing
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$, and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with generators $E_i,F_i,K_h$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). The lattice $P$ plays
the role of the integral weights of the classical theory
([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]); the pairing need not
be perfect, and no identification $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$ is
assumed anywhere.

A **$P$-graded type-one quantum weight module** is a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$
together with a direct sum decomposition

$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$$

(an internal direct sum of $\mathbb Q(q)$-subspaces, only finitely many nonzero
on each vector) such that, for all $\mu\in P$, $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $i\in I$,

$$K_h\ \text{acts on}\ M_\mu\ \text{by the scalar}\ q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle},\qquad E_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu+\alpha_i},\qquad F_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu-\alpha_i}.$$

The subspaces $M_\mu$ are the **chosen label-weight spaces**: the grading is
part of the structure and is not reconstructed from the action, because the
pairing may have a kernel. **Morphisms** of $P$-graded type-one weight modules
are the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps $f\colon M\to N$ with
$f(M_\mu)\subseteq N_\mu$ for every $\mu$; the weight submodules and quotients
considered on this page are those with the induced grading (Verification, steps
3.1 and 4.1).

The module is **integrable** if $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every
vector: for every $v\in M$ and every $i$ there are integers $N_e(v,i),N_f(v,i)\ge1$
with $E_i^{N_e(v,i)}v=0$ and $F_i^{N_f(v,i)}v=0$. The exponents may depend on
the vector and on $i$, and both directions are required independently;
integrability is not a uniform nilpotence condition.

The following are additional hypotheses, never part of the definition:
finiteness of the dimension of every $M_\mu$; boundedness of the set of $\mu$
with $M_\mu\ne0$ above (or below); finite generation of $M$. The zero module is
a $P$-graded type-one weight module with the empty grading ($M_\mu=0$ for all
$\mu$), and it is integrable.

Two remarks are recorded here and proved below. First, when the pairing
separates $P$, the spaces $M_\mu$ are exactly the simultaneous eigenspaces of
the $K_h$, and the present definition recovers the usual type-one weight
modules (Verification, steps 2.1 and 4.1). Second, when the pairing does not
separate, distinct labels $\mu\ne\mu'$ may carry the same toral character, and
a simultaneous toral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space;
the definition therefore takes the label grading as data. The regularization of
finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons on this page are proved
later, not assumed here by writing $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$.
No choice principle enters this definition.

Let $\lambda\in P$ be a dominant integral label weight, put
$m_i:=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$, and let $M(\lambda)$ be the quantum Verma
module with highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]],
[[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]).

(i) The quotient $\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$
is nonzero, has finite-dimensional label weights and support
$\lambda-Q_+$, is integrable, and equals the canonical simple highest weight
module $L(\lambda)$, which is simple also as an ordinary (not assumed graded)
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module.

(ii) **Universality.** Every integrable cyclic highest weight module $V$ of
highest weight $\lambda$ with highest vector $v\ne0$ receives a
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $\tilde L(\lambda)\to V$ with
$\bar v_\lambda\mapsto v$, and this map is unique; every nonzero such $V$ is
isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$.

(iii) Its character equals the classical integrable highest weight character of
the explicitly regularized realization of the datum. No global
$\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness and no crystal or global basis is used.

derivations.claim: **Toral relations.** Under $t\mapsto s^{-1}$ and $K_h\mapsto D_{-h}$, the library relation $K_hK_{h'}=K_{h+h'}$ becomes $D_{-(h+h')}=D_{-h}D_{-h'}$, and $K_0=1$ becomes $D_0=1$; these are the source toral relations. Toral elements commute in both presentations, so $\varphi$ is well defined on the toral subalgebra $\mathbb Q(t)[P^\vee]\to\mathbb Q(s)[\mathbb Z J]$.

**Mixed relations.** The library relation $K_hE_aK_h^{-1}=t^{\langle\alpha_a,h\rangle}E_a$ becomes, after $t\mapsto s^{-1}$, $D_{-h}E_aD_{-h}^{-1}=s^{-\langle\alpha_a,h\rangle}E_a$, and interchanging $h$ and $-h$ this is the source relation $D_{h'}E_aD_{h'}^{-1}=s^{\langle\alpha_a,h'\rangle}E_a$; the $F_a$-relation is the sign-reversed mirror. Throughout this pair the **source parameter** of the Fock-space literature is
written $s$ and the **library parameter** of the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra
[[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]] is written $t$; the
dictionary below sets $t=s^{-1}$.

Let $I$ be a nonempty consecutive set of simple-root indices and put $I^+=I\cup(I+1)$, the coordinate alphabet. On a finite coordinate interval $J=[k,r]\subseteq I^+$ the roots have indices $[k,r-1]$, the coordinate weight lattice is $\bigoplus_{a=k}^r\mathbb Z\delta_a$, $\alpha_a=\delta_a-\delta_{a+1}$ and $h_a=e_a-e_{a+1}$. The full central coordinate is retained. The source algebra $U_s$ has toral generators $D_a^{\pm1}$ for $a\in J$ and root generators $E_a,F_a$ for $k\le a<r$, acting on natural vectors $v_b$, $b\in J$, by

$$D_av_b=s^{\delta_{ab}}v_b,\qquad E_av_b=\delta_{a+1,b}\,v_a,\qquad F_av_b=\delta_{a,b}\,v_{a+1},$$

$$\Delta E_a=1\otimes E_a+E_a\otimes D_aD_{a+1}^{-1},\qquad \Delta F_a=F_a\otimes1+D_a^{-1}D_{a+1}\otimes F_a .$$

The library parameter $t$ is identified with $s^{-1}$; the **semilinear Hopf
dictionary** is the coefficient map $t\mapsto s^{-1}$ together with the
generator assignment

$$E_a\longmapsto E_a,\qquad F_a\longmapsto F_a,\qquad K_h\longmapsto D_{-h},$$

where the $E_a,F_a$ on the source side are the *divided* generators of the
source normalization and on the library side those of
[[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]] (the assignments agree on the
undivided generators $E_a=E_a^{(1)}$, $F_a=F_a^{(1)}$, and divided powers are
carried to divided powers because the quantum integers are invariant under
$q\mapsto q^{-1}$, [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]).
Root-label weights are preserved, while toral numerical eigenvalues use the
reciprocal parameter: on a weight vector of weight $\mu$ the library generator
$K_h$ acts by $t^{\mu(h)}=s^{-\mu(h)}$, which is the action of $D_{-h}$ because
$(-h)(\mu)=-\mu(h)$.

The **bar involution** sends $s\mapsto s^{-1}$, fixes $E_a$ and $F_a$ and
inverts each $D_a$; the corresponding library operation is the involution with
$t\mapsto t^{-1}$, $E_a\mapsto E_a$, $F_a\mapsto F_a$ and
$K_h\mapsto K_h^{-1}$ of [[def-the-bar-lattice-and-integral-lattice-of-a-based-module]]
and [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]].

The **natural highest weight** attached to an interval $[k,r]$ is
$\delta_k=\varepsilon_k$ (equivalently the highest weight reached by the
leading coordinate vector $v_k$), its **dual highest weight** is
$-\delta_r$, and the **fundamental wedge weight** is
$\delta_k+\delta_{k+1}+\cdots+\delta_m$ for $k\le m\le r$. Every fundamental
factor carries its own highest-vector-normalized bar, integral lattice and
divided-string crystal charts ([[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]]);
its internal antisymmetrizer embedding is primitive and integral but is *not*
asserted to be based in the library's raw lower $q_0$ chart. Infinite intervals
are defined by the compatible system of their finite subintervals, and
[[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]] with
[[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]] supplies
the library integrable modules used on each finite interval.

The source Fock families $L,T,P$ and the library form-dual upper family
([[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]]) will
be compared below through their actual forms; they are never identified by
their names.

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix
$$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$
the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

For all partitions $\lambda$ and $\mu$ of the same integer $n$,
$$\lambda\unrhd\mu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\mu'\unrhd\lambda'.$$

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $[\lambda]$ be its Young diagram
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A **tableau of shape
$\lambda$**, or $\lambda$-tableau, is a bijection
$$t:[\lambda]\longrightarrow\{1,2,\dots,n\}.$$
We write $t(i,j)$ for the entry of $t$ in the node $(i,j)$, and we display $t$
as the diagram $[\lambda]$ with each node carrying its entry. Thus a tableau
places each of the numbers $1,\dots,n$ in exactly one node of $[\lambda]$. For
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the diagram is empty and the empty map is the unique
tableau of shape $\varnothing$, the **empty tableau**. The **shape** of a
tableau $t$ is the partition $\lambda$ with $t:[\lambda]\to\{1,\dots,n\}$,
which is determined by $t$ because $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$.

**Standard tableaux.** A tableau $t$ of shape $\lambda$ is **standard** if its
entries strictly increase along rows and down columns, that is, if
$$t(i,j)<t(i,j+1)\quad\text{whenever }(i,j),(i,j+1)\in[\lambda],$$
$$t(i,j)<t(i+1,j)\quad\text{whenever }(i,j),(i+1,j)\in[\lambda].$$
The empty tableau is standard, because both conditions are vacuous, and it is
the unique standard tableau of shape $\varnothing$. Following the classical
notation we write $f^\lambda$ for the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux.

**The left action on tableaux.** For $\sigma\in S_n$ and a $\lambda$-tableau
$t$, define
$$(\sigma\cdot t)(i,j):=\sigma\bigl(t(i,j)\bigr)\qquad\bigl((i,j)\in[\lambda]\bigr).$$
Since $t$ is a bijection onto $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $\sigma$ is a bijection of
$\{1,\dots,n\}$, the map $\sigma\cdot t$ is again a bijection
$[\lambda]\to\{1,\dots,n\}$, hence again a $\lambda$-tableau, and
$\mathrm{id}\cdot t=t$, $\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot t)=(\sigma\tau)\cdot t$ for all
$\sigma,\tau\in S_n$: the rule is a left action of $S_n$ on the set of
$\lambda$-tableaux. For every $\sigma\in S_n$ the row sets of $\sigma\cdot t$
are the images under $\sigma$ of the row sets of $t$, and the column sets of
$\sigma\cdot t$ are the images under $\sigma$ of the column sets of $t$.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$,
with diagrams $[\lambda]$ and $[\mu]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For content counts
only, set $\mu_i:=0$ for $i$ beyond the number of parts of $\mu$; these
zeros are not additional parts of the partition.

A **semistandard tableau of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$**, also called a
semistandard tableau of shape $\lambda$ and **type $\mu$**, is a filling
$T:[\lambda]\to\{1,2,\dots\}$ of the boxes of $[\lambda]$ with positive
integers such that:

1. **content:** for every $i\ge 1$ the entry $i$ occurs in exactly $\mu_i$
   boxes of $[\lambda]$, so the multiset of entries is
   $\{1^{\mu_1},2^{\mu_2},\dots\}$ and in particular every entry lies between
   $1$ and the number of parts of $\mu$;
2. **rows:** the entries weakly increase along every row, that is,
   $T(i,j)\le T(i,j+1)$ whenever $(i,j)$ and $(i,j+1)$ are both in
   $[\lambda]$;
3. **columns:** the entries strictly increase down every column, that is,
   $T(i,j)<T(i+1,j)$ whenever $(i,j)$ and $(i+1,j)$ are both in $[\lambda]$.

The **Kostka number** $K_{\lambda,\mu}$ is the number of semistandard
tableaux of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$:
$$K_{\lambda,\mu}:=\#\{\,T:T\text{ is a semistandard }\lambda\text{-tableau of content }\mu\,\}.$$
This is well defined and finite: a filling of the $n$ boxes of $[\lambda]$ by
positive integers has at most $n^n$ possibilities for $n\ge1$ once each entry is required
to lie between $1$ and the number of parts of $\mu$, and conditions 1--3 cut this
finite set down to the semistandard tableaux, so $K_{\lambda,\mu}$ is a
nonnegative integer. It is zero when the conditions cannot be met.

Two entries may be equal inside a row, but never inside a column: a repeated
entry in a column would contradict the strict increase of condition 3, so the
repetitions of a label forced by the content $\mu$ must be spread across
distinct columns of $[\lambda]$. For $\lambda=\mu=\varnothing$ there is a
single filling, the empty one, so
$$K_{\varnothing,\varnothing}=1 .$$

**Relation to standard tableaux.** Because a tableau of content $(1^n)$ uses
each of the numbers $1,\dots,n$ exactly once, its entries are pairwise
distinct, and weak increase along a row is then strict increase along that
row; a filling of $[\lambda]$ with content $(1^n)$ is therefore semistandard
exactly when it is a standard $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]), that is,
$$K_{\lambda,(1^n)}=f^\lambda ,$$
the number of standard tableaux of shape $\lambda$. In particular, for $n\ge1$,
$K_{(n),(1^n)}=K_{(n),(n)}=1$, since the single row carries either the
standard entries $1,2,\dots,n$ or the $n$ copies of the entry $1$, and
$K_{(1^n),(1^n)}=1$, realized by the single column $1,2,\dots,n$ read from
top to bottom.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

derivations.claim: **Elementary fundamental modules.** On a finite coordinate interval $[k,r]$ let $W_n$ have vectors $w_S$ indexed by $n$-element subsets $S$. Put $D_aw_S=s^{\mathbf1_{a\in S}}w_S$, and let $E_a$ replace $a+1\in S$ by $a\notin S$, while $F_a$ makes the opposite replacement, both with coefficient one and zero otherwise. The toral relations follow from the changed coordinate; $[E_a,F_a]$ is $1$, $-1$ or zero on the three possible $a,a+1$ occupation patterns, exactly the toral fraction. Different-root mixed commutators vanish by the same replacement test. Distant replacements commute; for adjacent roots $E_a^2=F_a^2=0$ and $E_aE_bE_a=F_aF_bF_a=0$, since the last replacement encounters the already occupied endpoint. These are the adjacent Serre relations. Distinct subset weights are separated by the toral operators, and successive raising replacements take any subset to $\{k,\ldots,k+n-1\}$; lowering generates every subset from it. Thus this module is integrable and irreducible, of highest weight $\Lambda_{k+n-1}$, and is the fundamental module in the dictionary. The ordered wedge symbol denotes this model; the primitive antisymmetrizer realizes it integrally, without any assertion that the raw tensor lower chart makes that embedding based.

**Root rows and physical rows.** In column $j$ the root row runs from $k$ to $m_j$, whereas its physical height is $n_j=m_j+1-k$. The monomial therefore starts at $A(m_j,j)$ and descends through $A(m_j-1,j),\ldots,A(k,j)$. Its entries are strictly decreasing in that order and define a nonzero $w_S$ from step 1.1. Physical row $h$ means root row $k+h-1$; its row length is $\#\{j:n_j\ge h\}$. Hence the ordinary partition diagram is the conjugate of $(n_1,\ldots,n_l)$, not of the possibly negative multicharge. Column reading is a bijection to tuples of strictly decreasing entry blocks of these fixed lengths; the standard row inequalities are the corresponding semistandard inequalities.

**Weights and the vacuum.** The toral formula in step 1.1 gives precisely $\mathrm{wt}_j(A)$ and their sum on the tensor monomial. The ground column is $\{k,\ldots,m_j\}$, with weight $\Lambda_{m_j}$. Every other column weight differs from its ground by a nonzero element of the positive root cone: repeatedly raise its subset to the initial segment, decreasing its weight difference by a simple root at every step. The tensor top weight can therefore occur only when every factor is its ground vector. Its weight space is one-dimensional, spanned by $v_\Lambda$. This argument uses the explicit finite factor construction, not a yet unproved global-basis inclusion.

**The prefix order.** Use root dominance: a weight difference is nonnegative when it is a nonnegative integral combination of $\alpha_a=\delta_a-\delta_{a+1}$; on fixed-total-coordinate weights this agrees with the usual coordinate prefix criterion. Reflexivity and transitivity are immediate; equality of every factor-prefix weight forces equality of each column subset, hence of the column-strict tableaux, proving antisymmetry. If $A$ has $a$ in an earlier column $i$ and $b>a$ in a later column $j$, and $B$ swaps them, the prefix difference $\mathrm{wt}_{\le u}(A)-\mathrm{wt}_{\le u}(B)$ is $\delta_a-\delta_b=\sum_{v=a}^{b-1}\alpha_v$ for $i\le u<j$ and zero otherwise. Thus $A<B$.

**Infinite intervals.** Every fixed tableau differs from its ground only finitely many times. Choose an actual finite lower cut below all those changes, never an undefined $\inf I$ when $I$ is unbounded below, and a finite upper cut above all displayed entries and charges. Appending a common ground tail gives the same action of every root generator in the common subinterval: its adjacent occupation pattern is unchanged. The finite weight differences and all prefix comparisons are unchanged. The compatible union constructs the semi-infinite factors and tensor module; each fixed finite-support calculation is one of the finite computations above. Highest-weight uniqueness and the ground argument remain valid on those finite cuts.

**Conclusion.** The module, tableau labels, column monomials, root-coordinate weights and prefix order are well defined, and the vacuum is the unique normalized highest-weight tensor monomial. Ordinary physical partitions use the shifted column heights. All admitted consecutive intervals and multicharges are retained; no raw-chart basedness or additional choice is asserted.

source normalization and on the library side those of
[[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]] (the assignments agree on the
undivided generators $E_a=E_a^{(1)}$, $F_a=F_a^{(1)}$, and divided powers are
carried to divided powers because the quantum integers are invariant under
$q\mapsto q^{-1}$, [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]).
Root-label weights are preserved, while toral numerical eigenvalues use the
reciprocal parameter: on a weight vector of weight $\mu$ the library generator
$K_h$ acts by $t^{\mu(h)}=s^{-\mu(h)}$, which is the action of $D_{-h}$ because
$(-h)(\mu)=-\mu(h)$.

The **bar involution** sends $s\mapsto s^{-1}$, fixes $E_a$ and $F_a$ and
inverts each $D_a$; the corresponding library operation is the involution with
$t\mapsto t^{-1}$, $E_a\mapsto E_a$, $F_a\mapsto F_a$ and
$K_h\mapsto K_h^{-1}$ of [[def-the-bar-lattice-and-integral-lattice-of-a-based-module]]
and [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]].

The **natural highest weight** attached to an interval $[k,r]$ is
$\delta_k=\varepsilon_k$ (equivalently the highest weight reached by the
leading coordinate vector $v_k$), its **dual highest weight** is
$-\delta_r$, and the **fundamental wedge weight** is
$\delta_k+\delta_{k+1}+\cdots+\delta_m$ for $k\le m\le r$. Every fundamental
factor carries its own highest-vector-normalized bar, integral lattice and
divided-string crystal charts ([[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]]);
its internal antisymmetrizer embedding is primitive and integral but is *not*
asserted to be based in the library's raw lower $q_0$ chart. Infinite intervals
are defined by the compatible system of their finite subintervals, and
[[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]] with
[[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]] supplies
the library integrable modules used on each finite interval.

The source Fock families $L,T,P$ and the library form-dual upper family
([[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]]) will
be compared below through their actual forms; they are never identified by
their names.

Work with the type-$A$ coordinate lattice and the dictionary of
[[def-the-fock-convention-dictionary-for-finite-type-a-quantum-modules]];
weights are written in the coordinates $\delta_a=\varepsilon_a$.

Fix a set $I$ of consecutive residues (for the finite box model
$I=\{k_0,\dots,k_0+N-2\}$ and $I^+=I\cup(I+1)=\{k_0,\dots,k_0+N-1\}$; $I$ may be
unbounded below or above), a positive **level** $l$, and
$$\Lambda=\Lambda_{m_1}+\cdots+\Lambda_{m_l}\in P^+,\qquad m_1\ge m_2\ge\cdots\ge m_l,$$
where $m_j\in I^+$ and, if $I$ has lower endpoint $k$, $\Lambda_m=\sum_{k\le a\le m}\delta_a$. When $I$ is unbounded below, $\Lambda_m$ is the ground semi-infinite fundamental weight with the finite-coordinate-difference interpretation below. For $I$ bounded below put
$n_j=m_j+1-\inf(I)$ boxes in column $j$ and $n=\sum_j n_j$; for $I$ unbounded
below use semi-infinite columns with a common finite tail below, as explained
after the weight definition.

The **higher-level wedge-tensor Fock module** is
$$F(\Lambda):=V(\Lambda_{m_1})\otimes V(\Lambda_{m_2})\otimes\cdots\otimes V(\Lambda_{m_l}),$$
the tensor product of the fundamental modules of the dictionary item. When $I$
is bounded below, $V(\Lambda_{m_j})$ is the fundamental integrable highest
weight module of highest weight $\Lambda_{m_j}$ in the library algebra. When
$I$ is unbounded below, $V(\Lambda_{m_j})$ is the semi-infinite wedge
$\Lambda^{m_j+\infty}V$ with $V$ the natural module for the locally finite
type-$A$ algebra on $I$; its basis is the set of normally ordered wedges
$v_{i_1}\wedge v_{i_2}\wedge\cdots$ with $i_1>i_2>\cdots$ and the tail
$i_k=m_j+1-k$ for all sufficiently large $k$.

A **$\Lambda$-tableau** $A$ fills the diagram of $\Lambda$ — the columns
$1,\dots,l$ of heights $n_j$, with rows indexed by $I^+$ — with entries in
$I^+$; it is **column-strict** if in each column the entries strictly increase
from bottom to top and all but finitely many entries of row $i$ equal $i$, and
**standard** if in addition the entries weakly increase from left to right in
each row. Write $\mathrm{Col}^\Lambda$, respectively $\mathrm{Std}^\Lambda$,
for the sets of column-strict, respectively standard $\Lambda$-tableaux, and
$A_\Lambda$ for the **ground-state tableau** with row $i$ filled entirely
with $i$.

For $A\in\mathrm{Col}^\Lambda$ the **column monomial** is
$$M_A:=\left(v_{A(m_1,1)}\wedge v_{A(m_1-1,1)}\wedge\cdots\right)\otimes\cdots\otimes\left(v_{A(m_l,l)}\wedge v_{A(m_l-1,l)}\wedge\cdots\right),$$
with each wedge normally ordered (the entries strictly decrease from top to
bottom inside a column), and
$$\mathrm{wt}_j(A)=\sum_{m_j\ge i\in I^+}\delta_{A(i,j)},\qquad \mathrm{wt}(A)=\mathrm{wt}_1(A)+\cdots+\mathrm{wt}_l(A),\qquad \mathrm{Col}^\Lambda_\alpha=\{A:\mathrm{wt}(A)=\Lambda-\alpha\}$$
for $\alpha\in Q^+$. When a column is semi-infinite, the displayed sum means
its ground fundamental weight $\Lambda_{m_j}$ plus the finite sum of the
coordinate differences $\delta_{A(i,j)}-\delta_i$ over the finitely many
positions where $A$ differs from the ground state, evaluated on each
finite-support coroot or torus input; no divergent infinite coordinate sum is
asserted.

The **Bruhat order** on $\mathrm{Col}^\Lambda$ is defined by $A\le B$ iff
$\mathrm{wt}(A)=\mathrm{wt}(B)$ and
$\mathrm{wt}_1(A)+\cdots+\mathrm{wt}_j(A)\ge\mathrm{wt}_1(B)+\cdots+\mathrm{wt}_j(B)$
in the dominance order of [[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]] for every
$j<l$; then $A<B$ whenever $B$ is obtained from $A$ by swapping entries $a<b$
in columns $i<j$. The column reading of a tableau (list the columns from left
to right, each column read top to bottom) gives the passage to partitions and
to the Young-diagram conventions of
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]] and
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]; the removable- and
addable-node notation of [[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]
is used for the box moves of a tableau.

The vector $v_\Lambda:=M_{A_\Lambda}$ is called the **vacuum vector**. Weight
bookkeeping, the uniqueness of the monomial of weight $\Lambda$ and the
bijectivity of the column reading are verified below; the column-monomial theorem records the full integral tensor-basis statement. The well-definedness verification here constructs each fundamental factor explicitly without treating a citation to integrability as a wedge-basis theorem.

Let $M_1,M_2$ be chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight modules ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $M_1\otimes M_2$ carry the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module structure of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] given by the coproduct $\Delta E_i=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i$, $\Delta F_i=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i$, $\Delta K_h=K_h\otimes K_h$ of [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]. Then:

(a) **Grading.** $M_1\otimes M_2$ is a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module for $(M_1\otimes M_2)_\mu=\bigoplus_{\mu_1+\mu_2=\mu}(M_1)_{\mu_1}\otimes(M_2)_{\mu_2}$, a direct sum by [[thm-tensor-products-commute-with-arbitrary-direct-sums]].

(b) **Integrability.** If $M_1,M_2$ are integrable then so is $M_1\otimes M_2$: $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every pure tensor, hence on the whole module.

(c) **Finite weights and bounded support.** If in addition every label-weight space of $M_1,M_2$ is finite dimensional and each weight set is contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$, then the same holds for $M_1\otimes M_2$.

(d) **Tensored lattices.** If $(L_1,B_1),(L_2,B_2)$ are crystal bases of $M_1,M_2$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]), then $L_1\otimes_{A_0}L_2$ is a free $A_0$-submodule of $M_1\otimes M_2$ generating it over $\mathbb Q(q)$, satisfies $(L_1\otimes L_2)_\mu=\bigoplus_{\mu_1+\mu_2=\mu}(L_1)_{\mu_1}\otimes(L_2)_{\mu_2}$, and $B_1\otimes B_2$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $(L_1\otimes L_2)/q(L_1\otimes L_2)$ compatible with these weight decompositions.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\in P$ be a dominant integral label weight, put
$m_i:=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$, and let $M(\lambda)$ be the quantum Verma
module with highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]],
[[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]).

(i) The quotient $\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$
is nonzero, has finite-dimensional label weights and support
$\lambda-Q_+$, is integrable, and equals the canonical simple highest weight
module $L(\lambda)$, which is simple also as an ordinary (not assumed graded)
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module.

(ii) **Universality.** Every integrable cyclic highest weight module $V$ of
highest weight $\lambda$ with highest vector $v\ne0$ receives a
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $\tilde L(\lambda)\to V$ with
$\bar v_\lambda\mapsto v$, and this map is unique; every nonzero such $V$ is
isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$.

(iii) Its character equals the classical integrable highest weight character of
the explicitly regularized realization of the datum. No global
$\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness and no crystal or global basis is used.

Let $\lambda\in P^+$ and let $L(\lambda)$ be the simple integrable highest weight module with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$ ([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]); in this page we write $V(\lambda):=L(\lambda)$, following the notation of the crystal sources. Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half with its Kashiwara operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]), and let $A_0$ be the crystal limiting ring ([[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]]).

Define $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ to be the $A_0$-submodule of $V(\lambda)$ generated by all vectors $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda$ ($r\ge0$, $i_1,\dots,i_r\in I$), where for $r=0$ the vector is $v_\lambda$; and $\mathcal L(\infty)$ to be the $A_0$-submodule of $U_q^-$ generated by all $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}\mathbf 1$ ($r\ge0$), where $\mathbf 1$ is the unit of $U_q^-$. Here $\tilde f_i$ on $V(\lambda)$ are the module Kashiwara operators and $\tilde f_i$ on $U_q^-$ are the negative-half operators. Define
$$\mathcal B(\lambda):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda+q\mathcal L(\lambda):r\ge0\}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)/q\mathcal L(\lambda),$$
$$\mathcal B(\infty):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}\mathbf 1+q\mathcal L(\infty):r\ge0\}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)/q\mathcal L(\infty).$$

Then, with $\pi_\lambda:U_q^-\to V(\lambda)$, $\pi_\lambda(P)=Pv_\lambda$:

(a) $\mathcal L(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu$ with $\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu=\mathcal L(\lambda)\cap V(\lambda)_\mu$, and $\mathcal L(\infty)=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}$ with $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}=\mathcal L(\infty)\cap U_q^-[-\nu]$; correspondingly $\mathcal B(\lambda)=\bigsqcup_\mu\mathcal B(\lambda)_\mu$ and $\mathcal B(\infty)=\bigsqcup_\nu\mathcal B(\infty)_{-\nu}$.

(b) $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)$ and $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\infty)\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)$.

(c) (Recursive spanning.) For $\alpha\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$,
$$\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\sum_{i\in I}\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i},\qquad \mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\tilde f_i\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i}\Bigr)\setminus\{0\},$$
and the same formulas with $\mathcal L(\infty),\mathcal B(\infty)$. Each $\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$ and each $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha}$ is generated over $A_0$ by finitely many monomials of total length at most $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$, hence is a finitely generated $A_0$-module.

No basis property, scalar-extension spanning or crystal-lattice property of $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ or $\mathcal L(\infty)$ is asserted here; these are conclusions of the grand loop. The script letters avoid the collision with the simple module $L(\lambda)$. No choice principle is used. Each fixed component is torsionfree inside a field vector space and generated by finitely many words of its fixed height, so it is free over the DVR $A_0$; its full field-span is proved later. The field map $\pi_\lambda$ is surjective, but exact equality on Kashiwara monomial generators is not asserted.

Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ be crystals, meaning the data $(B,wt,\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i,\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i)$ attached to a crystal basis $(L,B)$ of an integrable module by [[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]] and [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]: $wt:B\to P$ is the weight function, $\varepsilon_i(b)=\max\{n:\tilde e_i^nb\ne0\}$ and $\varphi_i(b)=\max\{n:\tilde f_i^nb\ne0\}$ are finite, $\varphi_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle$, and $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ are the partial maps $B\to B\cup\{0\}$ of [[def-kashiwara-crystal-operators]].

The **tensor product crystal** $B_1\otimes B_2$ is the following data on $B_1\times B_2$, whose elements are written $b_1\otimes b_2$:

(i) $wt(b_1\otimes b_2):=wt(b_1)+wt(b_2)$;

(ii) $\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, and $\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=b_1\otimes\tilde f_ib_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2)$;

(iii) $\tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=\tilde e_ib_1\otimes b_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, and $\tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=b_1\otimes\tilde e_ib_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)<\varepsilon_i(b_2)$.

By convention a product is $0$ as soon as the operator applied to the selected factor is $0$; the **left factor is preferred** exactly in the displayed cases, so the assignment is left-to-right, matching the left-to-right order of the module tensor product $M_1\otimes M_2$ under the coproduct of [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]. The **equality case** $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ is split: $\tilde e_i$ acts on the first factor while $\tilde f_i$ acts on the second. The asymmetry is not free: with the same strict or non-strict comparison used for both operators the partial-inverse axiom fails, as the counterexample on the companion page records, while the displayed convention is internally consistent by the lemma on this page computing $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ of $B_1\otimes B_2$.

The functions $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ of $B_1\otimes B_2$ are read off from the two-case operators as maximal iterated powers, exactly as in [[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]. This definition only fixes combinatorial data and asserts nothing about an arbitrary pair of crystals: it does not claim that every such datum arises from a module tensor product. When $B_1,B_2$ are the crystals of crystal bases of integrable modules, the tensor product theorem later on this page proves that $(L_1\otimes_{A_0}L_2,\,B_1\otimes B_2)$ is a crystal basis of $M_1\otimes M_2$ with these operators, and only through that theorem are the values finite and nonnegative a priori. No choice principle is used.

Let $M_1,M_2$ be integrable chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight modules with crystal bases $(L_1,B_1)$, $(L_2,B_2)$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]), and let $M_1\otimes M_2$ be the integrable module of [[lem-tensor-products-of-integrable-weight-modules-are-integrable]].

Then $(L_1\otimes_{A_0}L_2,\,B_1\otimes B_2)$ is a crystal basis of $M_1\otimes M_2$, and its crystal is the tensor product crystal $B_1\otimes B_2$ of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]]: for all $b_1\in B_1$, $b_2\in B_2$ and $i\in I$,

$$\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\begin{cases}\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2),\\ b_1\otimes\tilde f_ib_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2),\end{cases}\qquad \tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\begin{cases}\tilde e_ib_1\otimes b_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2),\\ b_1\otimes\tilde e_ib_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)<\varepsilon_i(b_2),\end{cases}$$

with value $0$ as soon as the selected factor maps to $0$. In particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ map $B_1\otimes B_2$ into $(B_1\otimes B_2)\cup\{0\}$, and for all $b,b'\in B_1\otimes B_2$ one has $\tilde f_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde e_ib'$, so the partial-inverse axiom holds. The equality case $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ is resolved as in the definition: $\tilde f_i$ acts on the second factor and $\tilde e_i$ on the first.

No finite dimensionality, bounded support or uniform nilpotence is assumed, and no choice principle is used.

**Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module that is integrable, has finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight set contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]).

(i) **Splitting along the top isotypic part.** Let $\lambda$ be a maximal weight of $M$, put $N_0:=U_q(\mathfrak g)M_\lambda$ and let $N_1$ be the sum of the remaining simple constituents, so that $M=N_0\oplus N_1$ and $N_0\cong V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ with $m=\dim M_\lambda$. Then $L=(L\cap N_0)\oplus(L\cap N_1)$, $B=\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_0)/q(L\cap N_0)\bigr)\sqcup\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_1)/q(L\cap N_1)\bigr)$, and both pairs are crystal bases of $N_0$ and $N_1$.

(ii) **Uniqueness.** There is a locally weight-finite indexed family $(\lambda_j)_{j\in J}$ in $P^+$ and an isomorphism of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules $\Phi:M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{j\in J}V(\lambda_j)$ with $\Phi(L)=\bigoplus_j\mathcal L(\lambda_j)$ and $\Phi$ inducing a bijection $B\to\bigsqcup_j\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ of crystals. The multiset $\{\lambda_j:j\in J\}$ is the multiset of highest weights of the simple integrable constituents of $M$: the number of $j$ with $\lambda_j=\lambda$ equals the multiplicity $[M:V(\lambda)]$.

(iii) **Components.** Through $\Phi$ the connected components of the crystal $B$ are exactly the canonical highest weight crystals $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$; each component has a unique highest weight element $b$, of dominant weight $\lambda$, and equals the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]. In particular the crystal graph of any crystal basis of $M$ is determined up to isomorphism by $M$, and no other highest weight elements occur.

**Choice.** The axiom of choice is declared in [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and used to obtain the decomposition of $M$ into simple integrable highest weight modules from [[prop-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-modules-are-semisimple]], which selects a maximal independent family of simple submodules simultaneously. It also permits simultaneous choices of lifts of the finite residue bases in the possibly infinite family of top spaces. After those choices, each lattice and crystal argument is finite and choice-free. No incompatible-axiom branch is used, and no global $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness is assumed. The index set $J$ need not be finite in affine or indefinite type; local weight finiteness means only finitely many summands contribute to any fixed label-weight space.

derivations.claim: **The ordered-word lattice for one fundamental factor.** Define the exterior quotient by $v_a\otimes v_a=0$ and $v_b\otimes v_a=-s^{-1}v_a\otimes v_b$ for $b>a$. Thus sorting an ascending adjacent pair into descending order contributes $-s$, not a positive scalar. The coproduct sends a repeated-letter relation under $E_a$ or $F_a$ to the corresponding signed adjacent relation; on distinct letters the same two-term computation preserves that relation. Hence the quotient is a module. Sorting distinct letters has scalar $(-s)^{\ell(w)}$; commutation and braid moves preserve the number of inversions, and repeated-letter words vanish. The quotient therefore has one independent ordered generator for each distinct-letter orbit.

**The integral basis and primitive antisymmetrizer.** The quotient sorting relations have Laurent-unit coefficients and disjoint permutation orbits, giving a free ordered-word lattice. In the tensor lattice the alternating word of a descending tuple is the sum over permutations with coefficients $(-s)^{\ell(w)}$, with ordered coefficient one. Different tuples have disjoint supports; their span is a direct summand by taking the ordered coefficients and is therefore primitive. A coproduct replacement on the alternating sum cancels if it creates a repeated letter, and otherwise gives the alternating word of the replaced tuple with coefficient one; the two adjacent terms are exactly the cancellation checked in step 1.1. Thus sending an ordered quotient vector to its alternating word is an integral module isomorphism onto this span. No raw tensor-chart basedness is inferred.

**The wedge is the fundamental module with its own lattice, bar and crystal.** On ordered wedges the generators act by replacing a single entry: $E_av_b=\delta_{a+1,b}v_a$ and $F_av_b=\delta_{a,b}v_{a+1}$ on letters, extended multiplicatively to a wedge; an attempted replacement producing a repeated letter gives $0$. The top wedge is annihilated by all $E_a$ and is the highest weight vector; divided lowering powers reach every ordered wedge, so the wedge is generated as the integrable highest weight module $V(\Lambda_m)$ with highest weight $\Lambda_m=\sum$ of its ground letters, and the ordered-wedge lattice is its divided-power lattice with the induced bar involution and crystal chart.

**The tensor basis.** The tensor product of fundamental factors has as integral basis the tensor products of their ordered-wedge bases, i.e. precisely the column monomials $M_A$ with one wedge per column; by [F2] the tensor product is integrable and its weight is the sum of the factor weights, which is $\mathrm{wt}(A)$ as computed in [[def-higher-level-wedge-tensor-fock-module]]. This proves (1) and (2) on a finite cut.

**The lower-cut embeddings.** Appending the same entry $k-1$ below every column defines a linear map on the span of monomials; since the appended letters are smaller than every letter of the cut, the image is again a span of ordered wedges, so $\iota_k$ is injective and intertwines the common-root generator action: the appended letter is never moved by a generator whose residue lies in the cut, for the common root subalgebra. No assertion says the new boundary generator acts by zero: it may move the appended letter when the next letter is absent. The embeddings for decreasing cuts are compatible, and every semi-infinite tableau differs from the ground state in finitely many positions, hence belongs to the image of some lower cut and to some upper cut.

**Direct limit and finiteness.** The compatible system of the maps of step 5.1 with upper cuts containing all entries of the monomials gives the full Fock module as a direct limit; generators act by finitely many box moves because each generator replaces one letter in one factor, hence shifts the weight by a root and changes only finitely many entries; a fixed weight fixes the multiset difference from the common ground tail, so only finitely many tableaux occur and the weight space is finite dimensional. All finite-Cartan suppliers of [F2], [F3] are applied on the finite cuts, where every module involved is finite dimensional; no finite-dimensionality is claimed for fundamental factors on a merely lower-bounded infinite interval.

No biconditional is asserted; the statements are the existence of the integral basis and the compatibility of the embeddings.

citations.quote:
For any finite sequence of based integrable modules in the finite-weight-space category $O_{\mathrm{int}}$, the field tensor bar $\Psi=\Theta(\text{composite factor bars})$, built from the normalized intertwiner $\Theta$ of [[thm-the-weightwise-quasi-r-intertwiner-exists-and-is-unique]], is well defined, semilinear, $U$- and bar-compatible, involutive and independent of all parenthesizations; all root-height sums are vectorwise finite.

This field assertion holds for arbitrary based pairs and does not imply integral action. Its integral and based assertion holds for exactly the admissible cases proved by the integral-action supplier [[lem-quasi-r-divided-power-integrality-on-based-lattices]]: highest-first or first $C_{\mathrm{high}}$ with arbitrary based second; arbitrary based first with lowest or $C_{\mathrm{low}}$ second under finite action; all finite highest products and exact based subquotients and direct sums of their tensor constructions; ordered highest-prefix, based-middle, lowest-suffix products with explicit local support bounds; and arbitrary based pairs and products in finite Cartan type. For any other pair the same conclusion is conditional on an independently proved integral $\Theta$ action, not on field semisimplicity or lattice freeness.

In these cases: $\Psi$ preserves the divided-power integral tensor lattice; its action on raw tensor lower basis vectors is locally weight-transfer triangular with diagonal $1$; the actual tensor global vectors are its uniquely corrected bar-fixed lifts congruent to those raw tensor vectors modulo $q$, with corrections in $q\mathbb Z[q]$; they form a genuine $A$-basis and give the integral balanced tensor triple; the $q=0$ tensor lattice and crystal basis are supplied separately by the completed crystal tensor rule [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]], and the infinity chart is $\Psi(L_0^{\mathrm{tensor}})$, not an asserted bar containment in $L_0$, since semilinearity sends $q$ to $q^{-1}$. The raw tensor lower vectors are generally not bar fixed. Exact based integral and bar-compatible subquotient maps preserve the corrected global bases by balanced uniqueness. No assertion covers arbitrary two-sided-unbounded evaluation, semi-infinite limits, a universal-$R$ braiding, or general arbitrary-based integral action; the affine boundary in the supplier disproves the latter.

$\mathfrak p=\mathfrak l_J\oplus\mathfrak u_J$ and $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$
be as in [[def-parabolic-category-o-for-a-standard-parabolic]]. Then:

**(1) (Simples.)** Within an integral block, $L(\lambda)\in\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$
if and only if $\lambda$ is $\mathfrak p$-dominant integral; every simple
object of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ is of this form.

**(2) (Standards.)** For $\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$ the
generalized Verma $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ lies in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$,
has finite length, has $L(\lambda)$ as its unique simple quotient (head), and
$[M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):L(\mu)]\neq0$ forces $\mu\le\lambda$ in the
dominance order; $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ is the largest quotient of
$M(\lambda)$ lying in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$.

**(3) (Enough projectives.)** The inclusion
$\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}\subseteq\mathcal O$ is exact and has a left adjoint
$L_{\mathfrak p}$ (the largest $\mathfrak p$-locally-finite quotient);
$L_{\mathfrak p}$ is right exact and sends projective objects of $\mathcal O$
to projective objects of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$. Consequently, for every
$\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$ the object
$P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=L_{\mathfrak p}(P^{(\mathcal O)}(\lambda))$ is a
projective cover of $L(\lambda)$ in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$, and
$\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ has enough projectives and injectives.

**(4) (Generalized-standard flags, BGG reciprocity and duality.)** Every
projective in a fixed integral block has a finite generalized Verma flag. Its
projective cover surjects to its labelled generalized standard with a kernel
filtered by higher-labelled generalized standards. The simple and
generalized-standard classes form bases of the finite block Grothendieck
group, and characters are injective on this group. For $\mathfrak p$-dominant
integral $\lambda,\mu$,
$$(P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):M_{\mathfrak p}(\mu))=[M_{\mathfrak p}(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
the multiplicities being finite; moreover restricted duality restricts to an
exact contravariant involution of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ exchanging
$M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ and $\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$, and
$\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}}(M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda),\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\mu))=0$
for all $\lambda,\mu$.

A **finite Verma flag** of an object $X$ of $\mathcal O$ — also called a
**standard flag** or a **$\Delta$-flag** — is a finite increasing sequence of
subobjects
$$0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$$
such that each quotient $X_i/X_{i-1}$ is isomorphic to a Verma module
$\Delta(\mu_i)=M(\mu_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,n$. An object admitting such a flag is
called **Verma-filtered**. Since the flag is exhausted by its factors, its
class in the Grothendieck group
$K_0(\mathcal O)$ of [[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]
is
$$[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n[\Delta(\mu_i)].$$

For a Verma-filtered object $X$ and a weight $\mu$, the **multiplicity**
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is the number of indices $i$ with $\mu_i=\mu$ in a Verma
flag of $X$. This number is independent of the chosen flag by
[[lem-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-independent-of-the-flag]], so the notation
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is well-defined for Verma-filtered $X$.

flag of $X$ is exactly an isomorphism $X\cong\Delta(\mu)$ for a single weight
$\mu$, so the objects with a one-step flag are the Verma modules themselves.
The flag is a chain of subobjects of $X$ in the module category; it is not
required to split, and later examples show that it need not.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
